title: Man killed at Big Church Festival named as his church leads tributes
description: The man killed at a Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday has been named by his church as Robert Guanco, 41.He was a pastor at Jesus the Living
body: The man killed at a Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday has been named by his church as Robert Guanco, 41.He was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.Six other people were injured at the event by a falling sign at the Big Church Festival, near Steyning, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment.In a statement, his church said: "Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love, and his service to God will never be forgotten."On a fundraising page for the pastor's family, pastor Norman Ponce from Jesus the Living Water Worldwide Church, said Guanco was a "faithful servant of God"."What was meant to be a time of worship, fellowship, and celebration became an unimaginable tragedy," he added.Ponce said Guanco was a "beloved son, cherished brother, loving husband" and "great father"."He was also a good friend, mentor, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched," Ponce said."His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion, and service. "Through his ministry, kindness, prayers, and encouragement, he touched many lives."The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.The event at Wiston Park began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them."And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events."Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk , external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: WhatsApp group chat used to send millions in cash, funding crime and extremism
description: A WhatsApp group chat was used to send hundreds of millions of euros in cash around the world, funding organised crime and extremism with no paper tra
body: A WhatsApp group chat was used to send hundreds of millions of euros in cash around the world, funding organised crime and extremism with no paper trail, an investigation by European broadcasters has found.The 532-member group chat, called "Traders of Greater Europe", was used to arrange cash transfers across borders for their clients, including to British cities such as Birmingham and London.In one case, payments from Brussels went to militants from the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria.The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) investigative journalism network, external, which includes the BBC, also found wider evidence of similar cash transfer systems being used in people smuggling and drug trafficking.The group chat, which contained more than 82,000 messages sent between late February and December 2022, was first uncovered by Belgian investigating magistrate Vincent Guerra. An investigating magistrate is a judge who examines evidence in complex cases before trial and makes a recommendation about whether they should proceed.Guerra said the number of transactions was "staggering" and the network covered "the entire planet". The case began as an investigation into terror financing, but "it became just a drop in the ocean of transactions", he said.Members of the group chat sent messages in Arabic to each other to set up cash payments using the ancient hawala transfer system. Hawala involves a network of trusted money brokers who can arrange for funds to be sent around the world without any electronic record or physical transport of bank notes.The system involves an agreement between two brokers, known as hawaladars, in different locations. One of the hawaladars is paid a sum of cash and the other agrees to supply the same sum, minus commission, to the recipient. The hawaladars agree to settle up all their transactions between themselves at a later date.Hawala transfers are frequently used for legitimate purposes, such as immigrant workers sending funds home to support their families in countries with limited access to banks.But criminals can also take advantage of hawala transfers to avoid the Swift system used for most international money transfers, where banks typically flag large transactions outside the normal course of business and are required to report any suspicious activity.The Traders of Greater Europe group was reserved for transactions over €5,000 (£4,279) and payments were often much larger. There is no indication that all those participating in the group were involved in handling criminal funds.Hawala is illegal in many countries, including most of the EU, but is legal in the UK as long as the brokers are registered with Revenue and Customs (HMRC).The cache of WhatsApp messages was obtained by the EBU following a 2024 court case in Belgium which convicted six money launderers, including Abu Adam, the head of the network in Brussels, and his number two, Abu Ahmed.Belgian police had discovered evidence that the defendants had been sending money to IS, which was intended to help the wives of militants escape from detention camps in Syria. When they arrested Abu Adam, they discovered the Traders of Greater Europe group chat on his phone.Guerra said it was like "hitting the jackpot", uncovering the inner workings of a vast, underground system. The phone also contained 6,000 photos of €5 notes showing the serial numbers and 6,000 photos of identity cards. These details are often used as unique identifying codes in hawala transactions, and the total number of notes and ID cards suggest Abu Adam had processed at least 12,000 transactions, Guerra said."This isn't just amateur work; it's professional, and at a level we could never have imagined," he said. "They're bankers with no government oversight."The EBU also found further gangs across Europe using the hawala system for criminal activity. One former money launderer previously involved in European hawala networks, whom we are calling Frank, told the EBU he had been involved in transactions totalling several hundred million euros.His first introduction to the hawala system had been at an office in a small town outside Rotterdam, he said. There, five or six messengers had arrived with money in about an hour and a half, transferring at least a million euros, he estimated."What I found out later is that it's not just about money. It's about the financing of terror. It's about drug trafficking. It's about prostitution and all sorts of other crap, to put it nicely," he said.Cases in Austria have also revealed how the hawala system is bound up with people smuggling and violence.In one case investigated by Austrian broadcaster ORF, part of the EBU network, Austrian police raided what they called "the biggest hawala office in Vienna". It was run from a kebab restaurant on a busy thoroughfare and which authorities say was used to make payments for people smuggling.Two Syrian brothers who ran the operation were charged with human trafficking, as well as torturing and raping a courier who had lost €350,000 (£300,000), saying he had been robbed. They were convicted last year and sentenced to 18 and 8 years in prison respectively.Austrian police and Europol also recently dismantled another people-smuggling ring financed through hawala, which officials said had transported about 100,000 people into Europe over 18 months.Gerald Tatzgern, who leads human-trafficking investigations at Austria's Criminal Intelligence Service, the BK, told ORF that torture was a reality of people smuggling and was also used to maximise profits.He said: "Videos of the torture are then sent to the families, saying that if they don't send another €1,000 or several thousand euros, then the person concerned - your son, your brother, your father - will suffer."

schema.headline: WhatsApp group chat used to send millions in cash, funding crime and extremism

title: Lake Ontario sign installed in Canada in latest jab at US
description: Figure caption, Watch: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveils 'Lake Ontario' signByYang TianOntario Premier Doug Ford has hit back at Donald Trump by insta
body: Figure caption, Watch: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveils 'Lake Ontario' signByYang TianOntario Premier Doug Ford has hit back at Donald Trump by installing a large sign on Canada's shoreline with the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."The US president signed an executive order on Thursday seeking to change its name to Lake America and has shared a series of AI-generated videos about the lake that straddles both countries."Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ford said.The war of words was triggered after trade talks collapsed, with the US imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month.Figure caption, Watch: "He's losing it" - Americans react to Lake Ontario name changeTrump said the decree was effective immediately as he signed the order to rename it Lake America. While he has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks, other countries are not required to follow. Canadian officials have dismissed Trump's move.On Saturday, Trump also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, with one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one that says: "Welcome to Lake America."Another video depicted a flock of Canada geese sporting the US president's hair and holding rifles as they patrolled the shoreline of a newly named Lake America.Ford said Trump's renaming of the lake was because he "didn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves".Standing in front of the newly unveiled Lake Ontario sign, Ford added: "Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever."It echoes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's previous response to the row, insisting "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.When Trump entered the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

schema.headline: Lake Ontario sign installed in Canada in latest jab at US

title: PC Harper's killers to stay in jail as PM announces early release scheme changes
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the BBC that PC Andrew Harper's killers will remain behind bars as he announced changes to the early release sche
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the BBC that PC Andrew Harper's killers will remain behind bars as he announced changes to the early release scheme aimed at easing prison overcrowding.In an exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham said anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, would be excluded from the scheme, which would have made two of the officer's killers eligible for early release.Burnham said extra prison space would be created by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.It follows months of campaigning from PC Harper's family and former colleagues to block the release of his killers.The 28-year-old was responding to a burglary in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged along a road by a vehicle as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft.When it emerged that two of the killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, could be released early, there were passionate calls for the government to intervene and block those convicted of manslaughter from early release."I heard obviously what Andrew Harper's family were saying, I mean who couldn't? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison," Burnham told the BBC. He conceded the announcement would mean "hundreds" more people stay in prison, meaning additional space will need to be found in a system that is more than 97% full in England and Wales.Debbie Adlam, Harper's mother, told BBC Breakfast she welcomed the prime minister's decision."I am glad and really grateful that this has been the outcome for us, but I worry immensely for those it doesn't happen for," she said."And I think realistically, the overall system has left some huge gaps still."Harper's force, Thames Valley Police, said the announcement would be "welcomed by many across policing and our communities".Chief Constable Jason Hogg said in a statement, external he hoped it would bring reassurance to Harper's family, as well as to other victims and bereaved families "who continue to seek confidence that the most serious offences are treated with the gravity they deserve"."Today is not about politics," he said. "It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today."Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber said he was "pleased" Harper's killers would not now be released but added it was a "bittersweet victory".The Conservative politician also warned there had not been an "appropriate level of resources" provided to the probation service and the police to keep the public safe from people being released under the scheme.The prime minister said finding extra space would be achieved in part through ending Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences, or IPPs. These were available between 2005 and 2012, and were given to offenders who pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once a minimum term has been served, the prisoner can be released only once the Parole Board is satisfied they no longer need to be confined for public safety, meaning many are being held indefinitely. Burnham said he had applied "common sense" on the treatment of IPPs, which he had "long-standing concerns" about."I was faced with a situation where people on those sentences who have more than served their time, not being released when others who've committed very serious crimes being released early," he told the BBC."The judgement I've made is the public, in my view, would prefer a situation where people who have served their time to be considered for release before those who haven't."According to Ministry of Justice data, 2,271 people are serving IPP sentences as of June. Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so.Burnham conceded that of those offenders, there will be "individuals who will pose a risk to communities", and said a cross-party oversight group would be established.The government will table legislation to terminate the sentences by the "end of this Parliament", he added.Pressed on how many foreign prisoners could be returned, Burnham said it was "hundreds".The government has said powers will be implemented early next year to deport some foreign criminals immediately after sentencing. Those powers would block foreign prisoners from ever returning to the country while "keeping those in prison for the most serious crimes locked up for a substantial period before they are removed".The government is not thought to have signed any additional prisoner returns agreements with other countries.It is understood that work has also begun to create more cells in existing prisons by adapting space used for other purposes, but that is also expected to take months.None of the measures announced by Burnham are likely to create much additional prison capacity by the time the first batch of prisoners are released early in October.The prime minister is said to have taken a "political decision" to use some of the remaining capacity in the prison system to ensure the changes announced today could be implemented immediately.In addition to those in jail for manslaughter, the prime minister said prisoners convicted of indecent assault offences and death by dangerous driving will also remain in prison.Historic child sex offences and causing or allowing the death of a child will also be exempted from the early release scheme, while new "restriction zones" to better protect domestic violence survivors from perpetrators released early will be introduced. Burnham said the additional changes announced on Sunday would result in "hundreds" more prisoners staying behind bars.The justice secretary is expected to give a more precise figure for how many people will be affected when he gives a statement in Parliament on Tuesday.Earlier this month, Burnham announced prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would be excluded from early release eligibility.Dame Nicole Jacobs, Domestic Abuse Commissioner for England and Wales, warned that Burnham's announcement "won't bring reassurance" and said she remains "deeply concerned about the number of abusers who will still be eligible for early release"."Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot", she added.The Sentencing Act 2026 was designed to address the prisons overcrowding crisis, by releasing large numbers of inmates earlier than had been previously planned. The early release scheme is scheduled to start on 1 October.But it was met with fierce opposition from some, including family and former colleagues of PC Harper. Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020 and would previously have become eligible for release under the scheme after serving half of their sentences, down from two-thirds.The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was given an "extended" sentence of 16 years for manslaughter and was therefore not eligible for release.PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, had described the prospect of their sentences being reduced as "deplorable". Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp previously accused Burnham and Labour of "re-traumatising victims and their families with their constant U-turns".Liberal Democrat Justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said: "The uncertainty and distress caused by this government over the early release scheme is unforgivable."PC Andrew Harper's killers will now remain in prison, but this should never have been in question."During his early days as prime minister, Burnham announced the changes brought in by the Sentencing Act would be paused while a review was carried out. On 3 August, the government announced prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would be excluded from the new policy.Prisoners serving sentences for murder would not be eligible for early release.While Downing Street initially warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter, Burnham later said he was "confident" of being able to block PC Harper's killers from the scheme.It marked a shift from a week earlier, when he said there was "nothing more" he could do without risking the collapse of the prison system.The Sentencing Act made a number of key changes designed to mean fewer people were sent to prison, and to free many inmates earlier than planned.The prison population in England and Wales on 24 August was 86,843, which is 97.6% of the total capacity.Additional reporting by Jack Fenwick and Claire Keenan

schema.headline: PC Harper's killers to stay in jail as PM announces early release scheme changes

title: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
description: On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launc
body: On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled. Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it. It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents. The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long. Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

schema.headline: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there

title: Why some US restaurants are banning tips
description: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer get
body: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer gets tips but her salary is double the normBySuzanne Bearne Wine waiter Caroline Kraetzer earns $40 (£30) an hour, double what most service staff in San Francisco are paid but then it costs a lot to eat at her restaurant.At a set price of $140 (£100) per person, La Cigale is one of a small number of US restaurants charging higher prices so it can pay high salaries - and it doesn't allow tips.It tells customers: "What you see is what you pay. We do not accept tips, your kind words and return visits will suffice."Kraetzer says it is good to no longer be "reliant on the generosity of strangers to pay the bills".While waiting staff at other restaurants can make a lot of money from tips, she says "you're often there two hours before service, and again when you're closing after the guests have left, so you are making minimum wage during that time".Fairer for staff?On the other side of the US, Rachel Miller, chef and owner of Nightshade Noodle Bar in the town Lynn, Massachusetts, moved to a tip-free model five years ago when they reopened after the Covid-19 pandemic.Her motivation was to make it fairer for the kitchen staff. "The people breaking their backs and minds in the kitchen - often the least visible and the least celebrated - were taking home a fraction of what the front staff made on tips for the same hours," she says.Miller says she found it "deeply unsettling" to see higher tips going to white male staff and lower tips to everyone else. "Tipping lets guests, consciously or not, pay people differently based on gender, race, or sexuality and I was not willing to let that decide my team's income."To pay the staff higher wages, Miller also increased prices at the French-Vietnamese restaurant. Its tasting menus now start from $102 (£75) for seven courses before 18:00, and $126 (£92) for nine courses."Our prices are higher than a comparable restaurant's because they carry the full cost of paying people properly," says Miller. "That is the trade, and I stand behind it."Image source, Alyssa BlumsteinImage caption, Rachel Miller says that banning tips is fairer for her kitchen staffTip-free can mean higher pricesYet not every restaurant that has switched to a tipless model has made a success of it, as sometimes customers don't appreciate the higher menu prices.Talulla in Cambridge, Massachusetts, dropped tips in 2020 so it could pay staff more equitably, only to then switch back in September of last year."We tried to keep our non-tipping model simply by raising our menu prices 23%, but we were only able to sustain this through the winter months," says co-owner Danielle Ayer."Operating a non-tipped restaurant is more expensive overall," adds Ayer. This is because tips don't count as part of a restaurant's revenues, but higher menu prices do. So if a venue increases prices to pay staff more, its revenues go up accordingly, and it must pay more sales tax.William Michael Lynn, professor of food and beverage management at Cornell University and author of The Psychology of Tipping, says the problem of going tip-free is that customers struggle to get their heads around the maths."Higher menu prices make dining out seem more expensive because people do not adequately take into account that they are no longer tipping," he says. "It leads to lower demand."Image source, Amanda CohenImage caption, Amanda Cohen says customers are pleased when they realise they don't have to tipIn New York, vegetarian restaurant Dirt Candy was one of the very first to ban tipping back in 2015. "I wanted to make it more equal for everybody," says chef and owner Amanda Cohen, who now pays her staff about $30 an hour.She says that many customers "are pleasantly surprised when they realise they don't have to tip 20% on top".Cassidy Van der Kamp is a filmmaker whose YouTube documentary Tipless was inspired by her own experience of working in a restaurant in Oakland, California which went tip-free.While some other servers left, Van der Kamp, who was originally paid about $10 an hour plus tips, decided to stay and earned $21 per hour after the change."I had stability for the first time as I knew what I was earning… and I didn't need to look at a low tip and think what did I do wrong?"'Tipping fatigue'While Van der Kamp liked the move, Lynn says that a huge challenge of moving to a gratuity-free system is that it can be difficult to attract and retain waiting staff who like getting tips.However, given the growth of what has been called "tipping fatigue" – people being increasingly annoyed at having to pay high tips – will more restaurants stop the practice?"Despite tip-fatigue, I do not think tipping is going to be eliminated on widescale anytime soon because the economic disadvantages of eliminating tipping outweigh the advantages," says Lynn.Back at Nightshade Noodle Bar, Miller doesn't regret her decision. "The clearest measure is that staff stay."Turnover in this industry is brutal, and we have people who have been here since we made the change. It has proven to be highly valued by my guests and team."

schema.headline: Why some US restaurants are banning tips

title: England v Pakistan: Nasser Hussain calls early end to play at Lord's 'a joke'
description: The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nas
body: The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nasser Hussain.On a Saturday badly affected by persistent showers at Lord's, players left the field at 17:08 BST.At that point, prospects of conditions improving sufficiently for play to resume seemed remote. However, rain cleared and the sky brightened.The groundstaff partially removed the covers while officials deliberated. At 18:30, with up to an hour of playing time remaining and with the weather the best it had been all day, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned proceedings.The decision was greeted with booing by some of the sparse crowd that remained inside the ground."That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports."I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is."In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."The weather stayed dry and the light remained good up to 19:30, the time at which play would have been scheduled to close.The morning session had been washed out and only 24.5 overs of play were possible as the players dodged the showers, meaning spectators will receive a 50% refund on the price of their ticket.If 30 overs had been completed, spectators would not have been entitled to any money back.Still, the abandonment caused some fans to express their displeasure with messages to the BBC's live coverage of the Test."Sat in the Edrich Stand," wrote Joe at Lord's. "It hasn't rained for half an hour and it's as bright as it's been all day. Absolutely no justification for not playing right now. A real shame."Rachel in Kingswinford added: "Ridiculous to call it off! They want fans supporting Test cricket and those spectators have stuck with it all day - another 30-45 mins of play would have been a better look (plus saving authorities money on refunds)!"Another message from Paul in Northwich read: "This is a terrible advert for cricket. It's like the umpires are waiting for it to rain again. At least the spectators can get a refund."Play ended with England 177-7 in their second innings, 357 ahead and on course to win the match and series.Batting conditions had been difficult all day and it would have been another challenging period for the home side had they been asked to return for a short time late in the evening."It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50."It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward."Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."The situation at Lord's came on the same day Durham were denied the chance to chase a victory target of four against Gloucestershire because of bad light at the end of the third day of their County Championship match at Chester-le-Street.It means the teams will return on Sunday for what could be as little as one ball of action.Gloucestershire were dismissed for 250 in their second innings in the closing stages of Saturday, with visiting coach Mark Alleyne claiming the light was already too poor before his team were all out."I'm not sure where to start, really," said Alleyne. "I mean, 45 minutes before we lost the last wicket, it was too dark to play, which would have been consistent with all the other days that we played.""We had probably 50 minutes of cricket there that we probably shouldn't have done."The match could have been concluded had Gloucestershire chosen to bowl spin, only for the away side to refuse and push the game into a Sunday when rain is forecast."They asked if we would bowl our spinners to finish the game," added Alleyne. "Of course, we said no, we'll bowl our quick bowlers, in which case it became bad light, so we'll come back tomorrow."Durham coach Ryan Campbell wrote on X: "Cricket sometimes doesn't help itself. Before everyone loads up on the poor old umpires, it's not their fault."

schema.headline: England v Pakistan: Nasser Hussain calls early end to play at Lord's 'a joke'

title: Gamescom 2026: Highlights and developer insights from gaming's biggest showcase
description: I've been to Gamescom six times - here's what excited me this yearFigure caption, Watch: BBC's Laura Cress on the floor at Gamescom in CologneByLaura
body: I've been to Gamescom six times - here's what excited me this yearFigure caption, Watch: BBC's Laura Cress on the floor at Gamescom in CologneByLaura CressTechnology reporterGamescom is the largest in-person gaming event in the world, and this year it lived up to expectations with big games on show from The Witcher 3's new expansion, to Alien: Isolation 2.Last year over 350,000 people flocked to the halls of the Koelnmesse in Cologne, Germany to get a chance to see and play the most hotly anticipated games.This year that number of attendees is expected to have been even bigger, with the likes of Xbox and Sega showcasing games to the public alongside indie studios with only one or two developers.This was my sixth time attending Gamescom, which never fails to make me excited about the games industry. Here are a few of the big things I got to check out this week.The Witcher 3: Songs of the PastImage source, CD Projekt Red/Fool's TheoryImage caption, Gamers will once again play as the gruff-voiced Geralt of Rivera in the new The Witcher 3 expansionWhen CD Projekt Red announced it was making a new expansion for the hugely popular action-role playing game The Witcher 3, it came as a shock.The original, after all, came out 11 years ago.Yet it was clear sitting in the crowd for Opening Night Live on Tuesday that there's still a lot of love for the older game. There were gasps and audible shouts of joy when the team announced they were providing a free upgrade to the original.As for the expansion, Songs of the Past will follow the gruff-voiced protagonist Geralt in an adventure discovering more about the past of his close friend Dandelion.Doug Cockle, who voices Geralt, told me it was a "thrill" to return as The Witcher."I love this character so much...it's like slipping into a warm bath, or putting on an old pair of shoes," he said.Image caption, Doug Cockle, who plays Geralt, out of his Witcher uniform, alongside Laura CressFrom what I got to see, it's clear choice will once again be front and centre of the player's experience, with lots of options to choose from in how to react to people.For those hoping to take their time tossing a coin to their Witcher, the head of co-developer Fool's Theory Jakub Rokosz told me this expansion would be "on par with the size" of previous additions such as Blood and Wine and Hearts of Stone.Alien: Isolation 2Alien: Isolation 2 is the long-awaited sequel to Horsham-based Creative Assembly's 2014 survival-horror game.One of the things that made the original Alien: Isolation so terrifying was its seemingly intelligent Xenomorph, which appeared to learn from your behaviour and adapt to it.Considering I physically jumped out of my seat at one point playing the demo when avoiding the Alien, it's safe to say Creative Assembly will once again be ratcheting up the tension with the sequel.This time rather than playing as the daughter of Ellen Ripley, you play as Blake, a chief executive of the infamous Weyland-Yutani corporation. Image source, Creative Assembly/SegaImage caption, The Alien is as horrifying as everAs well as claustrophobic spaceship corridors, in the sequel you will also be avoiding the Alien in bigger, open air spaces. But the game's Project Art Director Anastasia Sopikova said that did not mean you would always feel safer."You step outside. And you're like, 'Oh yeah, I'm relieved, I'm outside," she said."And then the rain picks up and it gets foggier, and you hear something nearby and you're like, 'Oh, okay.' Suddenly you realise you're really vulnerable. You're really exposed."FableRalph Fulton, the founder of Leamington Spa-based Playground Games, told me the 2027 reboot of the role-playing classic Fable had "two tonal pillars" - "Britishness" and "fairy tales".Fulton said the team was keen to avoid the generic English accents often heard in fantasy games, pointing out that "accent is such an identifier in the UK, where accents change every 15 to 20 miles".Instead, Fable features voices from across the UK, and a voice cast of over 100 actors."I want to hear people from Newcastle, from Edinburgh, from Cardiff, you know? And we've done that and it brings this incredible sense of Britishness, and also this incredible sense of humour," he said.The game is deliberately not a continuation of the original trilogy's timeline, but it will have some of its quirks, taking players into a new open-world version of Albion - the game's fairy-tale version of medieval Britain.Tomb Raider: Legacy of AtlantisLara Croft has been exploring ancient ruins and culling the local wildlife for nearly 30 years now (the original Tomb Raider came out in 1996). Legacy of Atlantis revisits Lara's original adventure, including her journey through Peru.It's not the first time the classic game has been remade, but Jeff Adams, experience director at co-developers Crystal Dynamics, told me reimagining it was still a "very delicate formula"."You have to be very intentful with where you make modifications, but you do so in the attempt to kind of bring it into a modern gameplay space." As for why after 30 years people still want to play as the twin-pistoled adventurer, Michał Kuk, Creative Director at Flying Wild Hog, said it was not just about her athletic ability."It's also about the attitude, the energy, the self-confidence," he added.Image caption, They went all out with the Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis booth this yearElsewhere at the expo, over three days some got to take part in an event called Games Done Quick (GDQ), where people try to finish a game as quickly as possible.Its previous events are often watched by hundreds of thousands of people online, with GDQ's charity marathons having raised "62 million dollars for charities in the last 16 years", according to business director Ashley Farkas. "Anybody can be a part of this community, anybody can be a speedrunner, and it is just like a giant hug from gamers of like, hey, we want you to come, hang out and do fun stuff and raise money for charity," she said.Silent Hill TownfallSilent Hill, the psychological survival horror franchise from Japanese studio Konami, has for the most part been set in America, although the most recent excursion - Silent Hill f - was based in Japan in the 1960s era. Now in Silent Hill Townfall, made by the Glasgow-based team Screen Burn, that location is in an entirely new place - Scotland, albeit a fictional part of it - St Amelia.Image caption, Silent Hill's director says the game's setting is very ScottishScotland was initially going to be more of an influence than a setting, but the team ultimately decided to embrace it fully. Director Jon McKellan told me that approach felt "more natural and kind of authentic", with the game filled with recognisably Scottish shops and signage. "It's very, very Scottish," he said.

schema.headline: Gamescom 2026: Highlights and developer insights from gaming's biggest showcase

title: Harrison Armstrong: Everton call off transfer to Nottingham Forest after fan backlash
description: Everton's decision to reject Nottingham Forest's offer for teenager Harrison Armstrong has headed off the possibility of open revolt against owners Th
body: Everton's decision to reject Nottingham Forest's offer for teenager Harrison Armstrong has headed off the possibility of open revolt against owners The Friedkin Group from a furious fanbase.The revelation that Everton had received a £40m bid from Forest for the gifted 19-year-old, and it was under consideration, sparked an instant backlash from fans angry at the idea the club's best homegrown product for years could be sold.Instead, after a day of drama on and off the field, Everton's board - led by chairman and billionaire owner Dan Friedkin - decided to unanimously reject Forest's approach and keep Armstrong.Everton's fans made their feelings clear during the 1-1 draw at Bournemouth. The reaction was so loud, and toxic, that it is sure to have been heard by Everton's delegation at The Vitality Stadium and relayed back to the hierarchy in the United States.It is highly unlikely to be coincidence that a deal that looked to be advancing was then stopped in its tracks.And it will also pacify manager David Moyes, whose mood looked ominous post-match at Bournemouth, as he will now keep a young talent regarded as a key part of the club's future.Everton's supporters may reluctantly accept that important players could be prised away by clubs such as Manchester City - who have shown an interest in Iliman Ndiaye - but the notion of Nottingham Forest being able to do the same added another layer to their fury.Forest are one of the club's Everton and their fans would hope to surpass, not bolster them by selling one of their crown jewels to them.For The Friedkin Group, it is a PR catastrophe avoided.

title: Why young Brits are going to Japan
description: Mount Fuji pics, life-changing ramen and a weak yen - why young Brits are going to JapanImage source, Maitri SanghviImage caption, Seeing others' holi
body: Mount Fuji pics, life-changing ramen and a weak yen - why young Brits are going to JapanImage source, Maitri SanghviImage caption, Seeing others' holiday snaps of Japan on social media made Maitri Sanghvi want to go thereByGrace DeanAs I open up Instagram, I see another person in their late-20s has been to Japan.It shouldn't come as a surprise any more."I cannot scroll through TikTok or Instagram without seeing videos of people in [convenience store] 7-11 and trying all the different skincare and trying all the snacks and the viral sandwiches and the viral drinks and going to all the viral restaurants," says Alex Baker, who has been to Japan three times.There's been growing hype about Japan as a travel destination among young British people.Data from the Japanese National Tourism Organization, external shows that 483,157 British tourists visited Japan in 2025, up 24.8% on 2024 and up 40.8% on 2019, the benchmark year used by travel companies to compare with pre-pandemic trends. Provisional data for 2026 suggests numbers are continuing to grow.This reflects the boom in total tourism to Japan since the pandemic, with a record number of foreign visitors in 2025.The Brits in their 20s and 30s I spoke to gave a long list of reasons for wanting to go to Japan - the cityscapes, food, anime, nature, history, gaming, temples. But they largely agreed that social media was the main driving force behind so many young people heading there.When Maitri Sanghvi scrolled through TikTok, "Japan just kept popping up," she says.It was a big reason why Maitri, 24, and her boyfriend went for three weeks earlier this year. "Seeing [Japan] on social media restarted my urge of wanting to go," she says.Search #japantravel on TikTok or Instagram and you'll see countless videos of Mount Fuji, bowls of steaming ramen, itinerary suggestions, small villages in the Japanese Alps, the Fushimi Inari torii gates in Kyoto, the neon lights of Osaka's Dotonbori, and the chaos of Shibuya Crossing."Seeing other people's Japan videos definitely influenced my decision to go," says Aden Ibrahim, 29.Image source, Aden IbrahimImage caption, Aden says the social media buzz around Japan made him want to goSince he went with friends last July, Aden has posted dozens of TikToks of his trip, and he's still uploading them more than a year later. One captioned "Japan made it out the group chat" has 1.1 million views.Travelling to Japan isn't cheap - return off-peak flights with a layover in China start at about £450 with a budget airline. But the yen is weakening, making it cheaper for tourists when they're actually out there - even as rising prices hit residents. In July, the yen fell to a 40-year low."You can literally get a bowl of life-changing ramen for £3/£4 compared to a rubbish one here for like £20," says Faye Jawad, 26, who reviews restaurants on TikTok and visited Japan last year.Image source, Faye JawadImage caption, Faye says eating out in Japan was surprisingly affordable"When the yen was weakening, I thought 'actually this is a good time to go, things are going to be cheap'," says Vivek Haria, 26, who has a trip planned for this autumn. His interest in Japanese culture means he's wanted to visit for years - he has been learning the language and even sings in the UK-Japan Choir - but he says the value of the yen made it even more attractive.The low prices have led to many tourists splashing out on souvenirs when they're out there. Videos of people showing off their Japan "haul" of flavoured KitKats, stationery and clothes have become popular on social media.When Sam Corbett, 23, was in Japan in May he bought so many souvenirs - including snacks, matcha, clothes and skincare - that he had to buy an extra suitcase, which he stuffed full. Everything was "really affordable," he says.Image source, Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Many visitors talk about being entranced by Japan's convenience stores Almost all the Brits I spoke to had stuck to the same route known as the Golden Route: Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, often with day trips to nearby destinations like Nara, Hiroshima and Mount Fuji.It's easy to see why so many tourists pick this route. These cities are easy to travel between and packed with some of Japan's biggest attractions.But complaints about badly-behaved tourists are sparking debate about overtourism.Chiyuki Izumii, a tour guide for the Japan Guide Agency, feels tourist behaviour has got worse in recent years. She says that while her customers are respectful, she's seen other tourists jumping queues for buses, blocking space on board with big suitcases, carving their initials on trees in Kyoto's bamboo forest, speaking in loud voices at night and entering restricted areas to take pictures. Some authorities are cracking down. Fujikawaguchiko, a town near Mount Fuji, cancelled this year's cherry blossom festival after repeated issues with misbehaving tourists, while Tokyo's Shibuya ward, home to the famous Shibuya Crossing, started issuing on-the-spot fines for littering in June.In July, Japan increased its international tourist tax, external - typically incorporated into flight and boat tickets for people leaving Japan - from 1,000 yen (£4.60) to 3,000 yen, which it says will be spent on things like improving public transport and restoring historic sites.Image source, Shawn Goldberg/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty ImagesImage caption, Overtourism is a big topic of discussion in cities like KyotoSome visitors were surprised just how crowded major cities in Japan were."I was prepared for it to be busy but I didn't expect it to be as busy as it was," says Millie Dring, a huge anime fan who went in November with a friend to celebrate her 21st birthday. The DisneySea theme park near Tokyo was so busy that Millie and her friend only went on one ride, which had a three-hour queue, and felt overwhelmed by the crowds.Image source, Millie DringImage caption, Millie says cities like Tokyo were even busier than she expectedSam blames some of the crowds at tourist hotspots on social media hype and he says he regrets going to some places just because they were popular online. One dessert spot he went to in Kyoto after seeing it "all over social media" was very busy "and there wasn't a single local person in the queue," he says.Sites like the Hakone torii gates and Arashiyama bamboo forest had huge crowds of people trying to get Instagram-perfect photos, he says.But for some visitors, the hustle and bustle of the tourist destinations are all part of the attraction."I think there's a snobbiness around being a tourist over the past couple of years where people want to avoid looking like one," says Laura McGregor, 29, who's spending two weeks in Tokyo and Osaka in November for her honeymoon. Her plans include going to Disney and Universal, attending a sumo event, visiting Fuji and Hiroshima, and hiring go-karts to drive around Tokyo."Of course I want to experience an authentic side of Japan but I'm excited to embrace the tourist side too and go along with it," she says.

schema.headline: Why young Brits are going to Japan

title: Villa and Chelsea transfers: Why the clubs keep doing business
description: Chelsea have signed Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa for £7.5m - the eighth deal between the two clubs in the past four years.T
body: Chelsea have signed Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa for £7.5m - the eighth deal between the two clubs in the past four years.The 33-year-old, who won the World Cup in 2022, has moved to Stamford Bridge on a three-year deal.Former Arsenal goalkeeper Martinez joined Villa in 2020 and made 256 appearances, helping the club win the Europa League last season."I'm delighted to be at this football club," Martinez said. "Coming to Chelsea, for me and my family, was an easy decision to make and I'm just over the moon - I can't wait to get started.'I want to be successful here. I'm someone who wants to win at everything I do and I want to bring that here to this football club because it's a football club that wins titles, so I think it's a good match."Martinez's move to Chelsea comes after Nicolas Jackson's transfer the other way last week.No two Premier League clubs have exchanged more players, on permanent or loan deals, in the past four years.The relationship began after Chelsea's owners, BlueCo, took control of the club in 2022 and signed Carney Chukwuemeka from Villa for £20m that summer. Ian Maatsen (£37.5m, to Villa), Omari Kellyman (£19m, to Chelsea) and Axel Disasi (a £5m loan deal, to Villa) subsequently moved between the clubs.This summer alone has brought four more deals. Morgan Rogers completed a £117m move Chelsea, while Alejandro Garnacho joined Villa on loan with a conditional obligation to buy in a deal worth around £43m. Jackson then moved to Villa for £65m, before Martinez followed. Since 2022, Chelsea have paid Aston Villa £163.5m for players. Villa have spent £102.5m on Chelsea players including Axel Disasi's loan fee. That figure could rise to £150.5m should certain criteria be met to make Garnacho's loan move permanent. Chelsea believe the terms are easily reachable.Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali and Villa owner Nassef Sawiris have developed a close working relationship and have communicated directly over transfer business.That relationship has spanned several transfer windows and included Rogers' move to Stamford Bridge this summer. Chelsea did not have a clear run at Rogers, though - as Arsenal also wanted to sign him, and it was the player's decision to move to Stamford Bridge.Uefa has the power to scrutinise transfers completed between the same clubs within a 45-day period. Garnacho's move to Villa - on an initial loan deal - came two days after Rogers signed for Chelsea. Jackson's permanent transfer went through 38 days after the Rogers one.But a timeline on its own is not evidence that the deals were in any way related.Villa, for instance, could point to their long-held interest in Jackson, who previously worked with head coach Unai Emery at Villarreal. Chelsea, meanwhile, could argue their interest in Martinez was independent of previous dealings with Villa and would have been pursued regardless of the club he played for. The goalkeeper had attracted interest from Juventus earlier in the window, with a finger injury understood to have scuppered a move.

schema.headline: Villa and Chelsea transfers: Why the clubs keep doing business

title: We share a 15-acre mansion in Powys for cost of a two-bed house
description: The hall, which has served as a school and a care home as well as a former stately home over the years, now holds seven flats within its walls and a n
body: The hall, which has served as a school and a care home as well as a former stately home over the years, now holds seven flats within its walls and a number of communal living areas and shared facilities like washing machines and heating.Louise first came across Dol-llys after she was made redundant from her insurance job in London. She found herself spending more and more time away from the city, enjoying walking in the rural countryside, and realised she wanted to live there permanently."I'm a single person, so moving to a country village on your own is not that easy," she says. "Somebody mentioned [intentional] communities and said 'have you heard about them?'"After investigating quite a few, she knew she did not want to live somewhere where she only had a bedroom and everything else was shared. And at Dol-llys, where she moved in early 2020, she found the perfect combination of community and privacy."We term ourselves as co-housing, because we all have our separate flats," she says, and that the set-up is not a commune. "We share the grounds, we share the common rooms, we share responsibilities and decision-making, but we all have our front doors, which I think is important to everybody who chooses to live here."When Ken O'Brien and Susan Lancaster, both 70, began looking for a new start in retirement, one of the things that attracted them to Dol-llys, alongside its architectural merits and the plentiful grounds, was its record of success.The community began back in 1991. When Louise first moved in, one of the original members had been there for nearly 30 years.Ken, who had lived in a religious community as a young person, says of their search for cooperative living: "There were new ones, one that had high turnovers, ones that had a specific ethos, which this one didn't."It seemed mature, professional. People were organised. It was stable and well-run.""The house was in a very good state as well," Susan says. They moved in a few months after Louise.Ken adds: "We have common interests so we can do things together. But it's also the communal project – we're looking after the house and the grounds. We've got projects like growing so we like to think we can be a bit more resilient."Jemma, 36, originally from Birmingham, and her partner Yiannis had "always lived alternatively". They had first met while living in the Brithdir Mawr community in west Wales, then lived on a houseboat, and another community in Meifod, Powys, before applying for the one rental unit at Dol-llys."We were both always seeking an alternative but for us, especially in our early 20s, it was a really good way to get access to different role models, different ways of thinking. Things like permaculture, nature, those weren't necessarily things that we had time for or access to," Jemma explains."As well as all the benefits from working on projects and having your home life be quite vocational, it can be very practical as well. It can be a way to have a better quality of life."Jemma works in healthcare and has a 40-minute commute to a larger town – not unusual in rural mid Wales – and her partner is a support worker. Having a community-focused job is a common theme here, with several residents either current or former health, education and public sector workers.Membership of Dol-llys, apart from those renting, is on a loan stock basis with the community being equal shareholders, and residents pay a monthly service charge for group expenses and projects.They have a wood-fired boiler to provide heating, with solar panels providing some electricity and people are billed according to consumption.Everything is decided by consensus – such as installing solar panels - which Louise says can take time to get used in the beginning.When someone moves out, the co-operative looks at what they paid moving in then compares with national and local house price trends to decide on a fair percentage increase in value.Their website says a share now costs £230,000, with the right to live in a two or three-bedroom flat. Two to three-bedroom properties in the local town currently advertised range in price from about £110,000 to upwards of £250,000.Louise says: "We all grow veggies down there. We've got the chicken field. We've got eight acres of woodland. We've got the lake down there and we've got a huge field."The minimum commitment is one work day a month, at least one half-day of gardening, which is specific gardening maintenance as opposed to working on their own individual plots of land, and a half-day of processing wood to provide fuel for the communal boiler.They all learn the necessary skills when they move into the house if they do not already have them."I've got a chainsaw man turning up today to sell me a new one," says Louise. "I never thought I'd be doing that when I lived in London."Residents range in age from seven to 70. This summer, however, the balance will shift towards a younger demographic, as two older residents are leaving and two families with three children aged from six to 12 will be moving in.There is a four-stage application process to become a community member."We know that the more effort we put into the application process, the better chance it's going to work and it's going to be a good fit," says Louise.Jenny Kincova, 64, the longest current resident of nine years' standing, is one of those moving on to live in Llanidloes itself, like a number of previous residents.She says of her move to Dol-llys: "I was on my own. My girls had left home. I didn't just want to move to a place and not know anyone. Once I moved here, I was really excited by the prospect of communal decision-making and cooperative community living."Although she still enjoys the communal living, she has started to find the "emotional energy" needed for decision-making and keeping a group together tiring."I don't want to lose contact with here at all," she said."As you can see, we still get on, it's not about that at all. It's just about change again."I'm not going to have all this space and I'm not going to live in a listed building."The hall offers free allotments to locals in exchange for some help on their work days, holds open days, lets groups use its communal rooms for things like yoga classes, and will be holding its first board games weekend this summer. Its residents even gave the hall to friends for free to use as their wedding venue.It has recently hosted volunteer workers from the Wwoof (Worldwide Opportunities on Organic Farms) organisation, where people get free board and lodging for two weeks while helping out with projects in the grounds and learning skills.

schema.headline: We share a 15-acre mansion in Powys for cost of a two-bed house

title: Itauma vs Hrgovic: British heavyweight given a hard lesson on the realities of world-level boxing
description: It would be too simplistic - and unfair - to say Hrgovic won the fight purely through mind games, but the 34-year-old had succeeded in making the buil
body: It would be too simplistic - and unfair - to say Hrgovic won the fight purely through mind games, but the 34-year-old had succeeded in making the build-up uncomfortable.Hrgovic spent fight week repeatedly attacking Itauma's age, dismissing him as "just a kid". As the week wore on, Itauma looked increasingly irritated and eventually lost his composure at the weigh-in, shoving Hrgovic before the Croatian responded with a slap.Itauma prides himself on being unusually cerebral for a heavyweight. He reads psychology and self-help books, talks openly about sharpening his mind and appears to spend far more time analysing himself than most 21-year-olds.But there is always a danger that deep thinking becomes overthinking, something Anthony Joshua has been accused of repeatedly during the latter stages of his career.Whether the pre-fight barbs played any part or not, Itauma's gameplan once the bell rang was clear; he wanted to end the night early."Someone said to me he doesn't feel like he'd win a world title unless he knocks him out. I didn't like that," Warren said.That mindset was understandable because it had served Itauma extraordinarily well until now. But perhaps Hrgovic had been underestimated by almost everybody - Itauma, the media, pundits, former fighters and bookmakers who installed the Briton as a heavy favourite.Hrgovic is an Olympic bronze medallist who went 12 hard rounds with the giant Zhilei Zhang, while against Daniel Dubois - the only defeat on his record - he was leading on two of the three scorecards before the fight was stopped because of cuts.'El Animal' knew what it felt like to be hurt, to become tired and to remain in a fight when things were going badly. Itauma did not.Itauma showed that many of the qualities which looked spectacular against lesser opposition still worked against a genuine world-level heavyweight.He proved he can take a punch - there was no single blow that suddenly revealed a fragile chin. His hand speed troubled Hrgovic and he made the Zagreb fighter look slow.So with those positives in mind, where does he go from here?"Don't give up. Don't lose confidence. Get a few easy fights, easy wins. Build again and learn off these mistakes. You can't box like an amateur. It's a 12-round fight, you need to pace yourself," was Hrgovic's advice.Warren remains convinced that Itauma is one of the most exceptional talents he has encountered, pointing towards two-time world champion Dubois as a prime example of a heavyweight who rebuilt successfully after painful setbacks.But British boxing has seen the other side of that story too, of course - where fighters like David Price were once regarded as the country's next great heavyweight hope before successive defeats damaged an aura they never fully recovered.Audiences will now scrutinise Itauma's every move, his breathing and how he paces a fight. That vulnerability may actually make him a more compelling fighter to follow.The aura of untouchable perfection is gone. The schoolboy has been taught a lesson and now we will find out what he learns from it.

schema.headline: Itauma vs Hrgovic: British heavyweight given a hard lesson on the realities of world-level boxing

title: Newspaper headlines: 'We've not given up' and 'The X Backtop'
description: The Sunday Telegraph, external says John Healey is mulling a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in the Budget. Treasury officials are said to be
body: The Sunday Telegraph, external says John Healey is mulling a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in the Budget. Treasury officials are said to be looking at ways of plugging a £4.7bn black hole without raising direct taxes on individuals. The paper suggests banks and oil companies are seen as "low-hanging fruit". BP is said to have more than doubled its profits between April and June because of higher oil prices driven by the Iran war. In its editorial, the paper warns against the windfall tax move, saying it will harm growth by denting investor confidence.According to the Mail on Sunday, Russia is poised to target Britain with a cyber attack on a drone or missile factory. A key advisor to President Vladimir Putin, the former deputy foreign minister Andrei Fedorov, tells the paper the highest levels of the Russian government are considering such a strike. A drone factory owned by the British Ukrainian firm, Ukrspecsystems, is said to be a target. Its location, near RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, was made public in April.The Sunday Times, external reports that Andy Burnham has given what it calls a lucrative pay rise to train drivers on the Avanti West Coast London to Manchester line. The deal with union leaders was said to have been made to avoid strikes on a flagship service, and one of the busiest lines in Europe. The paper suggests industrial action would have proved embarrassing for cabinet ministers travelling to the prime minister's new political hub, Number 10 North, in Manchester.According to both the Sunday Telegraph and the Sunday People, new studies suggest statins can reduce the risk of dementia, as well as lowering cholesterol and the risk of heart attacks. The Telegraph reports that the largest study by Denmark's Copenhagen University Hospital found that the daily pills reduced the chances of dementia by up to 15%. The paper says the research means statins could benefit around six million of almost 10 million people aged 70 and over in the UK who are not currently taking them. The Sunday Mirror, external reports that Peter Homa, the ex-boss of Nottingham NHS Trust, where a review found that 520 mothers or babies suffered potentially avoidable death or harm, is now CEO of a firm giving maternity training to the health service. Grieving families tell the paper they are "concerned" by the news. Homa was approached for comment.The Sun on Sunday, external suggests the X Factor could return, seven years after it left our screens. ITV chiefs are said to be "in talks" about revamping the programme for a younger generation. The show's creator and former head judge Simon Cowell is said to be likely to return in some capacity.And several papers carry pictures of Sir David Beckham and his wife Victoria watching their son Cruz perform at the Reading Festival with his band the Breakers. "Beckstage at Reading" says the Sunday Mirror, external. "Band it Like Beckham" is the Sunday Times caption.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'We've not given up' and 'The X Backtop'

title: US Open 2026 singles preview: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz fare on comeback?

body: Fighting to stay No 1 - Sabalenka's US Open missionImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Aryna Sabalenka has won four Grand Slam singles titles, including two US Open victories in 2024 and 2025ByBBC Sport tennis news reporterAll was bright in Aryna Sabalenka's world when she completed a rare 'Sunshine Double' earlier this season.Becoming only the fifth woman to win the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back, Sabalenka emphasised her position as the dominant player on the WTA Tour and created a 3,000-point lead at the top of the world rankings.But a difficult period quickly followed - seemingly out of nowhere - leaving the 28-year-old Belarusian clinging on to her position going into the US Open, which starts on Sunday.Two-time defending champion Sabalenka returns to New York with a 17-7 win-loss record since the Miami triumph, including a chastening French Open quarter-final exit and a disheartening defeat in the Wimbledon fourth round.It is a record far below the four-time major winner's lofty standards.With 2,000 points to defend at Flushing Meadows and Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina now trailing by only 434, Sabalenka must win again to extend her 99-week run as the world number one.Asked if she felt confident she can rediscover her mojo on the hard courts on which she has thrived, Sabalenka said: "Absolutely. These tough lessons are definitely going to make me way, way stronger and working even harder."Sabalenka's four Grand Slam singles titles - two Australian Open and two US Open triumphs, all on hard courts - are more than most players can dream of.However, she has also lost four major finals and six semi-finals, despite a consistency on the biggest stages that is unrivalled among her peers.The concern in recent months has been Sabalenka's mental focus disappearing in less pressurised situations.This was most recently apparent in her Cincinnati Open fourth-round defeat by 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek. Sabalenka led 5-1 in a first-set tie-break and 4-1 in the second set, but continued to lack composure in the rallies as Bejlek rallied to win 7-6 (9-7) 6-4.At her previous tournament in Toronto, she lost to Russian world number 19 Ekaterina Alexandrova in the last 16 as her serve crumbled.During the clay-court swing, Sabalenka capitulated after winning the first set against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid, Sorana Cirstea in Rome and, most notably, Diana Shnaider at Roland Garros."I work on my mental side of the game. I've been trying to reset my mind and to come back stronger," a bullish Sabalenka said in New York."It's only a matter of time for me to come back."Who could take Sabalenka's crown?The drop-off in Sabalenka's results have opened the door for Rybakina, who beat the Belarusian to win the Australian Open in January, to take over as world number one.Rybakina might not even have to win a match at Flushing Meadows to do that, as she has fewer ranking points to defend than Sabalenka.However, there are questions over her fitness because of an ankle injury sustained in the Cincinnati quarter-finals.Rybakina can secure the number one ranking if her nearest rivals - Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - do not win the title.If Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still also rise to the top by reaching the semi-finals.Pegula, 32, has been ultra-consistent for several seasons without landing a major title, but the 2024 finalist hopes her runs to the Washington and Cincinnati finals will provide the platform for another crack at her home Slam.Gauff, who beat Pegula to the Cincinnati trophy last week, already has the experience of winning in New York after claiming her first major there in 2023. Twelve months ago, the 22-year-old American's game was clouded by uncertainty but returns with more confidence and fluidity in her serve.Beneath the leading quartet, the rest of the top 10 also hold either a Grand Slam or WTA 1,000 title - a group led by French Open winner Mirra Andreeva, Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and six-time major winner Iga Swiatek."You can just see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.Will someone take advantage of 'Sincaraz' injury issues?For the third Grand Slam in a row, the rivalry between Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has been put on hold.The pair swept all eight major titles between them in 2024 and 2025, with Alcaraz extending that run with victory at this year's Australian Open. But the pair have not competed at the same Grand Slam since. Alcaraz missed the French Open and Wimbledon with a wrist injury, and makes his comeback from a four-month absence in New York. A day after the 23-year-old Spaniard announced his plan to return, Sinner revealed he had been ruled out with a knee issue."It's kind of weird. We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months," said Alcaraz.Sinner's absence and the uncertainty around Alcaraz's fitness will galvanise the rest of the chasing pack - particularly 39-year-old Novak Djokovic.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Djokovic is a four-time US Open champion and reached the semi-finals last year, where he lost in straight sets to AlcarazThe Serb great, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, insists he has not put an "expiry date" on his extraordinary career. He continues to put himself in the mix for titles as he looks to finally land a standalone record 25th victory which would move him clear of Australia's Margaret Court on the all-time list.He has reached at least the semi-finals in six of the past seven Slams, but has not gone all the way since triumphing at the 2023 US Open.Germany's Alexander Zverev leads the seedings as he looks to reach a third straight major final, having won his first Slam at the French Open before losing to Sinner at Wimbledon.Canadian Open champion Ben Shelton and Cincinnati finalist Frances Tiafoe lead a strong American challenge, while 2024 finalist Taylor Fritz is another hope capable of ending a 23-year wait for a home men's champion.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 singles preview: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz fare on comeback?
